name: Süleymaniye Mosque
info: The Süleymaniye Mosque is the Ottoman imperial mosque on the Third Hill of Istanbul, commissioned by Suleiman the Magnificent and designed by Mimar Sinan, with an inscribed foundation date of 1550 and inauguration date of 1557.

facts.made: Commissioned by Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520–1566) and designed by the imperial architect Mimar Sinan; the foundation inscription was composed by Ebussuud Efendi and calligraphed by Hasan Çelebi
facts.form: A domed imperial mosque with a prayer hall of 58.5 by 57.5 metres under a central dome 53 metres high and 26.5 metres across, a courtyard of around 47 by 57 metres and four minarets, at the centre of a külliye (religious and charitable complex)
facts.where: On the Third Hill of Istanbul, Turkey, above the Golden Horn; part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Historic Areas of Istanbul"
facts.known: the largest Ottoman-era mosque in Istanbul; the central dome modelled on the Hagia Sophia; four minarets with ten balconies; restrained decoration and thuluth calligraphy; the mausoleums of Suleiman and Hürrem Sultan; the surrounding complex of madrasas, kitchen and hospital

t: Suleiman asked Sinan for a mosque of his own after the Şehzade Mosque, intending one that would surpass all those built by his predecessors and represent the pre-eminence of the Ottoman Empire.

Its prayer hall follows the dome-and-semi-dome plan of the Hagia Sophia and the Bayezid II Mosque, but Sinan hid most of the buttresses in the walls so that the outside rises towards the central dome.
The mosque stood at the centre of a külliye of madrasas, a hospital, a public kitchen and other buildings, and behind its qibla wall lie the octagonal mausoleums of Suleiman and Hürrem Sultan.
dyk: The four minarets have ten balconies in all, which is said to reflect that Suleiman I was the 10th Ottoman sultan.

sections.origins:
The Süleymaniye Mosque stands on the Third Hill of Istanbul, above the Golden Horn. Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520–1566) commissioned it and the imperial architect Mimar Sinan designed it. Suleiman had first chosen Sinan to build a mosque in memory of his son, Crown Prince Mehmed, and he was so impressed with the resulting Şehzade Mosque that he asked Sinan to design one for himself. This mosque was to represent the pre-eminence of the Ottoman Empire.

After the conquest of the Mamluk Sultanate by his father Selim in 1517, the empire covered much of the Islamic world, which encouraged Suleiman to define his role as an Islamic ruler. He was also in confrontation with the Safavids, a Shi'a dynasty in Iran, and forced them to make symbolic political concessions in the Treaty of Amasya in 1555. In this context he promoted the Ottoman state's reliance on the Shari'a, the ulama and orthodox Sunni ideology as a pillar of the sultan's authority and legitimacy. His intention was to build a mosque that would surpass all others built by his predecessors, and he appears at times to have represented himself as a "second Solomon". The Hagia Sophia, converted into a mosque in 1453, had remained an idealised symbol of sovereignty in Ottoman culture, which probably motivated him to emulate or surpass it.
sections.content:
The prayer hall is almost square, measuring 58.5 by 57.5 metres, and forms a single vast space dominated by its central dome, which is 53 metres high and 26.5 metres across, exactly half the height. The layout emulates the Hagia Sophia and the earlier Bayezid II Mosque: the central dome is flanked by semi-domes in front and behind, while a row of smaller, lower domes covers each lateral aisle, with large tympanas filled with windows between them. The entrance is preceded by a courtyard of around 47 by 57 metres with a central fountain and a colonnaded peristyle of marble, granite and porphyry columns. Four minarets stand at its corners; the two taller ones have three balconies and rise to 76 metres including their lead caps.

The interior decoration is restrained, and this seems to have been deliberate. The documents of the mosque's waqf (religious endowment) explicitly claim that ostentatious ornamentation of gold or jewels was avoided in order to conform with the traditions of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. The calligraphy is almost entirely in monumental thuluth script and is attributed to Hasan Çelebi. Iznik tile revetments are used only around the mihrab. The stained-glass windows of the qibla wall display the names of God, Muhammad and the four Rashidun caliphs, and these inscriptions emphasise the orthodox Sunni character of the mosque, reflecting in part the Ottoman rivalry with the Safavids.
sections.making:
The mosque was built on the site of the old Ottoman palace (Eski Saray), which was still in use and had to be demolished. The Arabic inscription above the entrance to the prayer hall gives a foundation date of 1550 and an inauguration date of 1557. In reality the planning began before 1550 and parts of the complex were not completed until after 1557: the final construction expenses were recorded in 1559, relating to some of the madrasas and to the mausoleum of Hürrem Sultan (d. 1558). Suleiman's own mausoleum was built after his death on the orders of his son and successor Selim II, between 1566 and 1568. Marble spolia from various sites in Constantinople and other parts of the empire were reportedly gathered and shipped to the site. Petrus Gyllius, a contemporary observer, wrote of seeing one of the four enormous porphyry columns destined for the interior being cut down to size, and of marble columns being taken from the Hippodrome.

Sinan repeated the innovations he had used in the Şehzade Mosque. The dome and semi-domes rest on a limited number of load-bearing pillars and buttresses, which allowed more windows and fewer divisions within the prayer space. He hid many of the buttresses in the outer walls and between colonnaded galleries, so that on the outside the arches, turrets and semi-domes form an almost pyramid-like progression to the central dome. The repetition of an older plan is uncharacteristic of Sinan and may have been the result of Suleiman's personal wishes.
sections.reception:
The mosque and its extensive facilities formed a political display of the sultan's power. Among other functions, it served as an impressive setting for the sultan's public appearances at Friday prayers. The waqf, the endowment deed of the complex, designated various religious officials who were to be closely associated with the Ottoman state, and the madrasas and other educational facilities were given a much larger staff than previous madrasas, which reflects Suleiman's promotion of the Shari'a and the ulama.

The building has been read against earlier ones. According to popular tradition, Justinian I boasted on the completion of the Hagia Sophia: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!" Suleiman's mosque in turn references the Hagia Sophia in its design and layout, and the mausoleum built behind it for Suleiman references the Dome of the Rock, which stands on the site of the Temple of Solomon. Some 16th-century writers noted the unusual courtyard fountain, which sprayed water from its ceiling into the basin below. The mosque is one of the best-known sights of Istanbul and is considered one of Mimar Sinan's greatest works. From the Third Hill it commands an extensive view of the city around the Golden Horn.
sections.survival:
The Süleymaniye was damaged in the great fire of 1660 and was restored by Sultan Mehmed IV. Part of the dome collapsed during the earthquake of 1766, and the repairs damaged what was left of Sinan's original decoration. Recent cleaning has shown that he experimented with blue before making red the dominant colour of the dome. In 1858 and 1859 extensive repairs were made to the interior, the minarets, the outer courtyard and the tombs. During the First World War the courtyard was used as a weapons depot, and when some of the ammunition ignited the mosque suffered another fire. It was not fully restored until 1956.

Between 1961 and 1967 the prayer hall was restored: 19th-century wall decorations were removed and earlier designs beneath the plaster were revealed and partly uncovered, restoring some of the mosque's 16th-century character, except for the central dome. Cement and gypsum-based mortars used in repairs between 1955 and the 2000s damaged the original structure, and in some repairs original decorations were partially or completely destroyed or painted over. The mosque was restored again between 2007 and 2010, the most comprehensive restoration undertaken in modern times. Original mortar, plaster and decoration were strengthened and preserved in place, cement additions were removed, corroded iron clamps were replaced with stainless steel, and cracks in the main dome were consolidated by injection-based reinforcement.
sections.legacy:
The Süleymaniye Mosque is the largest Ottoman-era mosque in Istanbul. The Süleymaniye Mosque and its Associated Conservation Area is one of the four components of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Historic Areas of Istanbul", protected under cultural criteria (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv); the area contains 920 registered properties. The present painting of the central dome dates from a 19th-century restoration by the Fossati brothers, who roughly imitated Ottoman Baroque decoration, and it has been maintained in recent restorations as it is now considered part of the mosque's history.

The mosque was designed as a külliye. The original complex consisted of the mosque, four madrasas, a primary school, a medical school, a hospital, a public kitchen serving food to the poor, a caravanserai, public baths, a school for the study of hadith and rows of shops, and many of these structures still exist. The former kitchen has been converted into a restaurant, and the former hospital is now a printing factory owned by the Turkish Army. Behind the qibla wall lie the mausoleums of Suleiman and Hürrem Sultan; Suleiman's also holds his daughter Mihrimah Sultan and the sultans Suleiman II and Ahmed II. The tomb of the architect Sinan stands just outside the complex walls to the north.

summary: The Süleymaniye Mosque is the imperial mosque Suleiman the Magnificent commissioned from Mimar Sinan on Istanbul's Third Hill, founded in 1550 and inaugurated in 1557. It followed the Hagia Sophia's dome plan, stood at the centre of a large külliye and was repaired after fires and earthquakes.
